Also, the shape of its pitch peaks fails to vary systematically with the information status of the phrase-final word. new_statements.quote: In a description of Ambonese Malay, van Minde (1997) assumed irregular word stress. No indications are given about the (default) location of word stress and, crucially, no report on the existence of schwa is provided (Paauw 2009). The main reason for irregularity is the phonemic nature of stress; hence the minimal pair /ˈba.rat/ ‘west’ and /ba.ˈrat/ ‘heavy’. However, a re-evaluation and acoustic measurements were carried out on read speech samples from four speakers (Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016). The samples were comparable to the ones in van Minde (1997) and led to the conclusion that word stress does not exist in Ambonese Malay.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey classification: Ambonese Malay has no word stress. Van Minde 1997 had claimed phonemic, irregularly placed stress with no default position; the acoustic study of Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (four speakers, read speech) found no reliable stress correlates in duration, F0 peak alignment or spectral tilt, reanalysed the 'unstressed' /a/ of the minimal pairs as a separate phoneme (a-caduc), and found no pitch accents either. p. 129 adds: 'Ambonese Malay was shown to lack word stress (Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016), counter to the P;U (LEX) claim in van Minde (1997). A small effect of spectral tilt could be found, but no systematic acoustic differences due to stress in duration or F0.'
new_statements.exceptions: Kaland (p. 97, sec. 4.1.2) cautions that the 2016 no-stress analysis rests on a small number of speakers and that van Minde's evidence was impressionistic minimal pairs; he calls for further empirical work but adopts the no-stress reading throughout.
new_statements.identity_note: van Minde 1997 describes 'Malayu Ambong', the Malay of Ambon town and island; Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 worked from four Ambonese Malay speakers reading material comparable to van Minde's (per Kaland 2025 p. 15). Paauw 2008's stress sentence is about reconstructed Vehicular Malay / North Moluccan Malay, not Ambon specifically. Erniati 2019 (not opened) is titled as the Ambon dialect of Malay.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (classification no-word-stress) rests on Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (Phonology 33(2): 353-389), an acoustic study that found no evidence for word stress or pitch accent in Ambonese Malay, seconded by Kaland 2025 (held, read). Van Minde 1997 (like his 1990 article) asserts the opposite type: phonemic, lexically unpredictable word stress with minimal pairs (b'acang/bac'ang, p'arang/par'ang, t'are/tar'e per pp. 21-23 via Wikipedia). The difference is one of analysis, not of variety: Kaland 2025 sec. 2.1.1.2 p. 15 reports that the 2016 re-evaluation with acoustic measurements did not confirm van Minde's stress claim. The bibliography row tags this work 'refines'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Van Minde describes Ambonese Malay as having phonemic word stress whose position in the word is lexically unpredictable (marked with ' before the stressed vowel in all transcriptions); monosyllables are treated as neutral for stress; suffixation can shift stress (l'aU ~ l'aUtan, i.e. onto the new penult). This is an impressionistic descriptive claim; the snippets give no default position and no acoustic evidence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing visible in the snippets (a 'secondary stress' search-within-volume probe by an earlier checker was blocked, not reachable by automated download); the 1990 lead article marks every accent in lexically reduplicated/compound forms but states no secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: monosyllables neutral as regards stress (p. 22); stress shift under affixation, e.g. /l'aU/ ~ /l'aUtan/ (p. 23) and 'stress-shift from final to penultimate syllable' (p. 28 snippet reported by the earlier locate pass); final unstressed syllables condition /i~e/, /u~o/ alternations (pp. 27-28, 33 snippets).
new_statements.identity_note: van Minde 1997 (and his 1990 Cakalele article) describe Ambonese Malay as spoken in the Bay District of Ambon Island and the Lease islands (Christian villages; fieldwork 1986-1989); Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 measured read speech of Ambonese Malay speakers. Same language (ambo1250); the disagreement is analytical, not dialectal. The work is not evidence about Banda Malay (band1353): 'Banda' occurs only in its historical introduction (earlier readers' snippet check).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): its position within the word is not predictable and is therefore marked (') before the stressed syllable in every polysyllabic transcription throughout the grammar; monosyllables are treated as neutral for stress and left unmarked. A morphologically conditioned stress shift under suffixation is noted (l'aU 'sea' ~ l'aUtan 'deep-sea', p. 23).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress visible in the snippets available.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables neutral/unmarked for stress (p. 22); lexically reduplicated morphemes carry a stress mark on each root (p. 22, snippet truncated); stress shift l'aU ~ l'aUtan under -tan (p. 23). The transcriptions visible in other snippets (t'obu, b'obo, pap'iñu, mar'iñu, bas'ar, bat'ul, kat'ong, bal'ong) show both penultimate and final stress in the lexicon, consistent with the 'unpredictable' statement; no default-penult statement is visible in the snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: van Minde 1997 describes Ambonese Malay (Malayu Ambong) as spoken on Ambon (and the Lease islands, e.g. Saparua appears in the term cloud); it is the Glottolog reference grammar for ambo1250 itself, not another Malay variety. His p. 202 remark about unresolved word stress concerns Indonesian, not Ambonese Malay.

readall_conflicts: The only substantive disagreement is the known one: van Minde 1997 (pp. 21-23, seen here only through Wikipedia's page-cited paraphrase and Kaland 2025's summary) describes phonemic, unpredictably placed word stress with minimal pairs (/'barat/ 'west' vs /ba'rat/ 'heavy', /p'araN/ 'machete' vs /par'aN/ 'war'), and Paauw 2008 (p. 99) repeats the pre-instrumental view for the eastern varieties generally (penult, final if the penult had schwa, phonemic after schwa loss). Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (catalog deciding source; abstract plus the open erratum) found no acoustic correlates of stress or pitch accent in four speakers and reanalysed the minimal pairs as a segmental /a/ vs weak /ă/ contrast; Kaland 2025 (pp. 15, 18, 97, 129-131) adopts that no-stress reading while noting the small speaker sample. the listed work (van Minde) could not be opened, so its stress statement remains verified only second-hand. The one work of this item, van Minde 1997 (read only through held Google Books snippets, pp. 21-23), states that Ambonese Malay has phonemic, lexically unpredictable word stress; the catalog codes the language no-word-stress on the strength of Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (acoustic study: no word stress, no pitch accent), a coding Kaland 2025 (held, read earlier) endorses while explicitly reporting van Minde's claim as not confirmed instrumentally. So the work contradicts the catalog on type (lexical stress vs no stress); this disagreement is already on record i…

Consequently, stress is not indicated in these forms. In what I call lexically ...' | p. 23: '... stress-shift is attested in: /l'aU/ 'sea' - /l'aUtan/ 'deep-sea' Section (3.2) gives more details on ...'

sources.note: The only reference grammar; source of the competing 'phonemic word stress' claim (pp. 21-23) that our the secondary-stress rule cites via Wikipedia only; needed to quote the impressionistic account first-hand and to check what van Minde actually says about default stress position.

sources.note: Silent on Ambonese Malay stress placement; repeats the pre-2016 descriptive assumption (phonemic penult/final stress inherited from schwa loss) for the eastern varieties as a group and presupposes 'unstressed' final syllables for Ambon after van Minde. Impressionistic; does not bear on the instrumental no-stress finding.

sources.citation: Paauw, Scott H. 2008. The Malay contact varieties of eastern Indonesia: a typological comparison. PhD dissertation, State University of New York at Buffalo. (already held by the project, symlinked)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No independent stress analysis for Ambon Malay: speaks of /i/~/e/, /u/~/o/ alternation 'in final unstressed syllables of polysyllabic morphemes' following van Minde (1997: 25-29); the explicit 'loss of the schwa has led to the development of phonemic stress ... ba'rat heavy / 'barat west' statement (p. 99) is made for North Moluccan/Vehicular Malay, with Ambon said to have undergone 'similar' processes. Impressionistic, pre-2016; aligns with the van Minde srule, not with the deciding instrumental result.
